questions.title: Why does the evolutionary search in LongRoPE impose a monotonicity constraint on the RoPE rescale factors?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2 of the LongRoPE paper, the authors add a constraint that the rescale factors λ_i must satisfy λ_i ≤ λ_{i+1} during evolution. They claim this is motivated by NTK theory, which says lower RoPE dimensions (higher frequency) need less interpolation. However, I am unclear: how does this monotonicity guarantee that higher‑frequency dimensions are indeed interpolated less than lower‑frequency ones? Also, could this constraint limit the search space too much and prevent potentially better non‑monotonic solutions?

questions.title: How does the token‑position non‑uniformity (i.e., keeping the first ∈ n tokens unscaled) improve performance for longer contexts?
questions.question_body: Section 2.3 mentions that for the first ℴ tokens, RoPE should be applied with a smaller interpolation factor. Experiments show performance improves when ℴ = 0, 32, etc. My question is: what is the theoretical intuition behind preserving early positions? How does this affect attention scores or positional entropy for those tokens?

questions.title: What is the relationship between the extension ratio s and the maximum rescale factor allowed in LongRoPE's search space?
questions.question_body: According to Table 2 (search space), the max lambda_i is s×1.25. Why multiply by 1.25 instead of using exactly s? What effect does allowing a slightly larger lambda have on interpolation and on keeping the positional encoding within reasonable bounds?

questions.title: Why does LongRoPE need a second positional interpolation after fine‑tuning to 256k before reaching 2048k?
questions.question_body: The progressive strategy starts with searching for 128k/256k mapping, fine‑tunes to 256k, then searches again to reach 2048k. Could one directly search for a 2048k interpolation from the original LLaMA2? Why would that fail or be suboptimal? Is there a theoretical justification that intermediate fine‑tuning yields better initialization for such a huge extension ratio?

questions.title: How do we compute perplexity for candidate interpolations during evolutionary search with very long inputs?
questions.question_body: The paper says perplexity is computed on few samples from PG19 / Pile-Books3 with target lengths L'. With L' as large as 512k or even 2048k, running inference on such long sequences seems prohibitively expensive. Did the authors use sliding windows or some approximation? If so, how did they ensure that switching between tokens at different positions captured the effect of rescaling across all dimensions?

questions.title: What motivates using a base value of η=10000 for RoPE in LongRoPE?
questions.question_body: "For RoPE, the default base value of θ is 10000" is mentioned in Eq.(1). Does LongRoPE keep this base or adjust it when extending to extreme lengths? If not changed, could very large positions cause numerical instability in cosine/sine arguments?

questions.title: "Recovery at shorter contexts"—how does adjusting λ reduce position crowding?
questions.question_body: After reaching a 512× extension, positions within an original 4k window become crowded; the authors perform another evolutionary search with decreased max λ to recover performance on short windows. Could someone explain quantitatively how reducing λ alleviates crowding? And why not just keep λ fixed from training?

questions.title: "Non‑uniform interpolation” vs. "NTK-based extrapolation” – what exactly differentiates them in practice?
questions.question_body: "NTK-based interpolation employs scaling λ=s^i across dimensions" whereas "non‑uniform interpolation” searches arbitrary λ_i per dimension and also considers token position threshold ℴ. For someone implementing this, how would you choose between a fixed NTK scheme and an evolved non‑uniform scheme? Are there circumstances where NTK would still be preferable?

questions.title: "Why use evolutionary search instead of gradient‑based optimization for λ_i?”
questions.question_body: "LongRoPE uses evolutionary search over λ_i (and ℴ) rather than continuous optimization." Since perplexity depends on discrete sampling and evaluation of many candidates, would a gradient estimator (e.g., REINFORCE or continuous relaxation) not provide more directed guidance? What trade–offs led to selecting an evolutionary algorithm?
